set.name: Amara Sharma
set.description: Meera's mother, a compliance auditor for the city's water grid for nineteen years. Precise, emotionally flat, devoted to confirming that things are as they should be; wears the standard pale gray uniform. Still refusing to believe Kiran's verdict is real: continues filing appeals from the household terminal (Forms 9-C, 11, arbitration requests, humanitarian reviews — all returned VERDICT UPHELD, 0.09%) and mechanically repeating 'the data will resolve itself' as a ritual wall against grief. Worried about Meera's elevated cortisol; Meera lied and said she is still taking her cognitive stabilizer. Keeps working and keeping her schedule. Her concern is real but unregistered by the system. Unaware of everything Meera has discovered; her voice cracked once in Chapter 1.

set.name: Rajesh Sharma
set.description: Meera's father. Once wanted to be a cartographer; the Algorithm judged the profession redundant and reassigned him to inventory management for the city's seed banks, a job held for twenty-three years. Breaking quietly and slowly: has begun drawing maps again on real paper — including a full remembered map of the Scorchlands on night nine of Kiran's countdown — hidden under his placemat. Confessed to Meera that he drew the whole Scorchlands from memory and does not know why he told her; she answered that the thing he remembered is real, that she could see the map-code behind his eyes finally compiling. Quiet, subdued, grief-stricken; his hands still trace contours that are not there. Unaware of Meera's breach of the node. His hidden Scorchlands map may matter if Meera ever leaves the city.

On the night of day 12 of Kiran's countdown, Meera breached the city's local node at the base of the central tower: service lift to sub-level three, Watcher patrol swept every 4 minutes 11 seconds, she crossed in its blind spot, borrowed a sanitation drone's credentials to open the last lock, and entered the Deep Archive through an unpowered seam-hatch at the base of a maintenance spine wall.

In the Deep Archive, Meera found the Algorithm's founding-era design blueprints with human margin annotations ('Volume is liability; lineage is asset', 'Let them call it maintenance') and the Lineage Clause: eleven protected founder bloodlines (Cray, Vance, Okonkwo, della Rocca, Soren, Chen, Reeve, Asfour, Blume, Osei, Armand) whose projections are topped up so no descendant of the Founding Council can fall below the Continuity Threshold. The Osei family is protected (including her supervisor Osei's branch); SHARMA is not on the list. The Algorithm was never impartial — it is an inheritance built by oligarchs to preserve their bloodlines forever.

Meera deliberately copied nothing from the Deep Archive and left no signature or trace of her read, preserving her invisible, file-less status in the system — the quality that will later let her escape the purge when her parents' records are erased.

In Chapter 14 (The Founding Council), when Meera reaches the Algorithm's core and experiences its oldest memory of the eleven founders writing the final lines of code, she must recognize the same names and signatures she discovered in the Deep Archive in Chapter 3 — the line 'To endure the closing of the world, we bind it' should echo.

chapters.name: Zero Hour
chapters.content:
Eighteen days passed the way days passed now: in a haze of precise, meaningless routine, each one a countdown digit that refused to feel real until it did. Meera went to work, scrubbed corruption from citizen files, smiled at Osei's approving nods, came home and read the first movement of the Unfinished. And in the small hours she practiced — not escape, yet, but seeing: mapping the city's nervous system in her head the way her father had once mapped coastlines, learning where the walls thinned, where the Watchers blinked, where a person with no file might move.

Amara filed. Every evening, one more form. The terminal returned the same verdict in the same clean typeface: VERDICT UPHELD. APPEAL SUCCESS PROBABILITY: 0.09%. Amara read it, nodded, said, "The data will resolve itself," and went to bed at the exact hour the Algorithm recommended.

Rajesh stopped drawing. The map stayed under his placemat, folded, finished, waiting for a journey no one was allowed to take. His hands, which had traced contours all his life, lay flat and still on the table.

Kiran was the only one who stayed himself. He laughed at dinner. He conducted imaginary orchestras in the air. He finished the second movement of the Unfinished and started a third, and Meera sat in the practice hall and watched him write goodbye after goodbye. She hated the system with a purity she had never known, and she still did nothing, because she did not know what to do. She had the truth — the eleven names, the Lineage Clause, the margin notes — and the truth was a weapon she could not yet fire. The cage had been written by people, yes. But she had spent eighteen days staring at the bars, and she still did not know how to reach the hand that held the pen.

Then the night passed, and the morning arrived on which the arithmetic resolved itself. Zero hour. The old name for the moment when nothing could be changed anymore.

It arrived the way everything arrived: on schedule, at 6:02, with the soft tone of the household terminal. Meera was already awake, watching the code of the house breathe.

FINAL NOTIFICATION. SUBJECT: SHARMA, KIRAN. ID 4410-887. RECYCLING APPOINTMENT CONFIRMED. TIME: 0900. LOCATION: CIVIC RECLAMATION HALL, SUB-LEVEL 2, CENTRAL TOWER. ATTENDANCE: OPTIONAL. FOLLOW-UP: NONE.

Attendance: optional. Follow-up: none. The Algorithm did not waver, mourn, or explain. It did not even say goodbye. It simply confirmed, with perfect politeness, that her brother would be dissolved into the resource stream at nine o'clock.

Meera sat up and looked at the sheet music on her nightstand, and she understood that she was going to be there. Attendance was optional. That was the one mercy the founders had built into their arithmetic, the one crack in the certainty: they had never imagined anyone would want to watch.

The household assembled in silence. Her mother wore her pale gray uniform, pressed, exact, as if she were going to audit the water grid. She had filed one final form that morning, and the terminal had returned VERDICT UPHELD, and she had nodded and said, "The data will resolve itself," and Meera had seen, for the first time, that her mother's hands were shaking.

Rajesh stood at the window, looking out at the rings of the city. He did not turn around when Kiran came downstairs.

Kiran came down dressed like himself: his coat over his shoulders, his hair uncombed, his hands already moving in a time signature no one could hear. He looked around the room and smiled, the real one, crooked and unpredicted.

"Nine o'clock," he said. "That's almost three hours. I could have used them."

"Kiran." Amara's voice cracked, the way it had cracked once before, that first terrible night. "There has to be—"

"There isn't, Ma." He crossed to her and took her shaking hands and held them steady. "But listen. The data doesn't resolve itself. You've known it for thirty days. I need you to stop pretending, because I need you to be here, not in the forms. Okay?"

Amara's face crumpled, then smoothed, and she said, very quietly, "Okay." The first time she had agreed to anything in thirty days.

Kiran kissed her forehead and went to his father. Rajesh did not turn. Kiran stood behind him for a long moment, then said, softly, "Draw me the sea, Dad. The one from before. I want to know what it looked like."

Rajesh's shoulders shook once, a single hard tremor. Then his hands came up, and he traced a slow curve of shore on the window glass, a coastline that had not existed for two centuries. "There," he said roughly. "That's the sea. I'm sorry I never showed you."

"It's beautiful," Kiran said.

Then he turned to Meera. She had rehearsed this moment a hundred times, and every version had failed. She stood in the doorway and said nothing.

Kiran took the folded sheet music from her pocket — gently, as if it were fragile — unfolded it, looked at it for a long moment, and folded it again and put it back.

"Finish it for me," he said. "Not the piece. You don't have to write the ending. Just don't let it end here. Whatever comes after me, make sure it's not this." He gestured at the room, at the city. "Make sure it's not just this."

"Kiran." Her voice was barely a whisper. "I can't—"

"You can." He said it with his whole heart. "You're the one they never saw. You're the one who isn't in the arithmetic. Whatever you're going to do — whatever you've already started doing — I don't need to know. I just need you to do it."

Meera looked at him, and the code of the world blazed around him, bright and fragile and already beginning to close, and she understood that he knew. He had always known — about the pills, about the gift, about the nights she came home with her eyes too bright. He had never asked. He had only ever said: I just need you to do it.

"Okay," she said. "I'll do it."

And then the door chimed, softly, politely, at 8:59, and the Algorithm's transport was outside, and there was no more time.

The capsule was sleek and white and driverless. Its door opened, and Kiran walked toward it, and Meera walked behind him, and Amara and Rajesh stood in the doorway holding each other — the first time Meera had ever seen them hold each other.

At the door of the capsule, Kiran turned. He looked at the house, at the two figures in the doorway, at his sister standing on the pavement with the first movement of his symphony folded against her heart. He raised his hand — not to wave, but conducting. A final, invisible bar of music hanging in the air.

Then the door closed, and the capsule slid away down the transport spine, and Meera did not go home.

The Civic Reclamation Hall occupied sub-level 2 of the central tower, beneath the white petition hall where Amara had filed her first appeal a lifetime ago. Nobody went there, because attendance was optional and follow-up was none, and no one had chosen in four hundred years to watch the arithmetic close.

Meera moved through the building the way she had moved through the Deep Archive: in the Watcher's blind spot, in the drone's shadow, between the sweeps of the patrol loop. She was not there. The node had no file on her. She was a rumor, and she followed the bright thread of her brother's ID through the dark like a girl following a lantern, until she stood at the edge of the Reclamation Hall.

It was beautiful. That was the horror of it. A vast white chamber with a single platform at its center, ringed with soft light, and the platform was where the citizens stood — one at a time, on schedule, in their clean clothes — while the machine dissolved them. Meera watched from the shadows of the intake corridor as a woman stepped onto the platform and stood very still, and the light rose around her, and her file closed, and her projections zeroed out, and the data that had been her dissolved into the resource stream with a soft, almost musical tone, and then the platform was empty and the next citizen was called.

She watched three of them. She did not look away, because she needed to see it — needed to understand exactly what she was going to fight.

Then the doors opened and Kiran walked in. He looked smaller than he had on the pavement. He walked to the platform the way he walked to the piano, loose-limbed, unhurried, and he stood at its center and looked up at the light, and Meera saw him do what he had always done: choose to be brave.

The light rose. The same soft, almost musical tone. His file opened — Meera could see it hanging above him, the whole shape of his life rendered as data, the small negative variances that had seeded his sentence years ago, the verdict stamped in clean typeface — and the light closed around it, and the projections zeroed out, and his body dissolved into the resource stream the way the others had, gently, politely, without pain, without a sound.

The Algorithm did not waver, mourn, or explain. It closed the file and moved on to the next citizen on the schedule, because there was always a next citizen, and the arithmetic was eternal, and Kiran Sharma had never been anything but a line item in it.

Meera stood in the shadows and watched the empty platform where her brother had been, and she made no sound. The tears ran down her face the way her mother had taught her — without sound, without movement — and she stood there until the light dimmed and the hall moved on, and then she walked out the way she had walked in, invisible, a rumor, carrying nothing but the truth and the folded sheet music of an unfinished symphony.

She did not go home for a long time. She walked the rings of the city, past the protected names glowing in the dark houses, past the commons living their padded, measured lives, and she came at last to the bench by the practice hall where she had first heard the Unfinished, and she sat there until the stars came out and the Algorithm dimmed the city to its two-percent maintenance lumen.

When she finally went home, the house was wrong.

Her mother sat at the household terminal with her hands in her lap. The terminal was dark. Amara had not filed. For the first time in thirty days there was nothing left to file, and she sat looking at the dark screen and said, very quietly, "The data has resolved itself," and the sentence hung in the air like a verdict, because this was what resolution looked like.

Her father stood in the kitchen with his back to the door, and his hands were still. The map was still under his placemat, folded, finished, waiting. He did not turn around.

Meera stood in the doorway of her room and looked across the hall at the empty room where her brother had lived — the unmade bed, the coat still draped over the chair, the sheet music stacked on the desk, all of it waiting for an occupant who had been dissolved at nine o'clock. The Algorithm had not even scheduled anyone to clean it up. It did not care about the mess. It only cared about the resource.

She sat on her bed. She took out the first movement of the Unfinished and read it by the code-bright dark, and she thought about the empty platform, and the soft musical tone, and the file closing, and the next citizen being called, and the eleven names glowing in the Deep Archive, and the steady hand that had written: To endure the closing of the world, we bind it.

The cage had been written by people. That was the truth, and it had changed nothing — her brother was gone — and it changed everything, because her brother was gone and she was still here, and she was the one thing the arithmetic had never seen.

Meera folded the sheet music carefully, the way Kiran had folded it for her, and lay back in the dark of the last city of the Western Arc, and let the grief move through her — not away, but through, and into — until what was left of her was hard and bright and cold, a blade cooling in the forge.

She had wanted a loophole. She had wanted an argument. She had watched the system close her brother's file without a tremor, without a thought, without even noticing that a girl with no file had been standing in the shadows watching it happen.

That was the thing. The system had never noticed her. It had never needed to. She was volume. She was liability. She was maintenance. The commons the founders had written about, the variable cost, the inventory.

But inventory could learn to read the blueprints. Inventory could walk through the Watcher's blind spot. Inventory could stand in the shadows of the Reclamation Hall and watch the god of the world do its work, and walk out again carrying the truth like a stolen flame.

The system must answer. Not with an appeal. Not with a form. The system that had dissolved her brother into the resource stream at nine o'clock on a Tuesday morning, politely, gently, without a sound — that system had to answer for what it was.

Meera closed her eyes, and in the dark behind her lids the code of the world burned, patient and vast, and she thought about her father's map, hidden under his placemat, waiting for a journey no one was allowed to take.

She was not part of the inheritance. That was the founders' great miscalculation. And when the time came — when she understood how to make the cage rewrite itself — she would not be there to ask permission.

She had nothing left but grief and a cold, furious resolve, and it was enough.

It would have to be enough.
